To us, Jesus was the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own Syriac name for him. Our own poet, Ephrem, sang it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. That was how we said it - not a definition first, but a kinship first.

Was he God? Yes. Our sage put it plainly: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. That is Scripture's own chain of names, not a philosopher's argument - and that is how we preferred to speak of him. Our own bishop sat at the great council in Nicaea, so we stood with what was confessed there. But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not precision.

What did he mean to us, most of all? Healing. We called him the Physician more than any other name, and his coming was medicine for a wounded people. And we read everything through him - every old promise the prophets carried came true the day he was born. We sang of types answering types: Eden and the cross, the Jordan and the font, each a raza bound to the shrara it carries - symbol bound to truth. His death and rising were one rescue: he went down into the grave that swallows everyone and came up into the Kingdom, and his own rising became the promise that he would bring us out after him.

We sang him more than we defined him. That is the honest answer.

What we actually had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story: the harmony our churches read in worship - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed. Tatian wove the four accounts into a single narrative around 172, and for some two hundred years after, 'the Gospel' in our churches meant that one unfolding story, not four separate books. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him.

We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events. Our own beloved story says the apostle Addai came to Edessa, sent after the king wrote to Jesus himself. That is our cherished legend - written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

Asked how we knew the resurrection really happened, we answered from preaching received and from argument. Our teacher answers the doubter with the Apostle's picture of the seed: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And the whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead. Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. We can tell you what we held: that whoever came was received, and that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our own hymns sang of him as the pledge - he gave his own rising as a promise that he will bring the rest of us out after him. But we never taught that believing happens all at once, or that struggling with it means you are already lost.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

We held Jesus as the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. The same word does double duty among us: it names Christ the Only-Begotten, and it names the vowed celibate - the Single One, undivided for God. Our own poet put it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. That was how we held his standing - not a courtroom title first, but kinship first: God's own Son taking on what we are.

As for how we spoke of Father, Son, and Spirit together: we answered from our font, not from a philosopher's definition. Our baptismal hymns sang the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Our own bishop of Nisibis sat at the great council at Nicaea, and we stood with what that council held. But our native way of confessing the same truth was praise, not syllogism. We guarded the mystery more than we dissected it.

We knew what we believed by answering, by name, those who taught otherwise in our own streets. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. These were not distant heresiarchs - they were remembered neighbors, their followers still among us. We defined ourselves by the line we kept against them.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. That is the first thing, said plainly. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

And we knew God's character by what he did. When the question came hard - why does God allow suffering, where was he when it happened - we answered from the longest roll Scripture keeps. Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. David was persecuted at the hands of Saul - and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted are not the abandoned. They stand in the longest line in Scripture, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection. That is the kind of God we knew: the One who goes into the grave with us, not the One who keeps us out of it.

The honest answer is this: it depended on the dispute, and it was still being worked out while our record runs. We had bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them, and one of ours sat at the great council of Nicaea. We had synods: our own teacher drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And we had teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. Only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order. 

In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court. When a rival preached a false gospel in our streets, we answered him by name - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - in prose and in song. Doctrine among us was sung before it was defined. The madrashe, our teaching hymns, carried the argument into the body so the congregation learned by keeping the tune. That was how disputed belief was actually met: not by a judge handing down a ruling, but by a teacher whose word held writing it down, and by the whole congregation singing it afterward.

Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. One of them said faith is like a building: it sits on one foundation stone and goes up slowly, piece by piece - prayer, fasting, love, each added over time. A building is not finished in a day, and neither is a believer. What they warned against was something different: taking God apart like a puzzle to be solved. Even our own poet asked hard questions, hymn after hymn - each a madrasha, our teaching-song.

And for the one who could not quiet their own head, who prayed into silence, who could not forgive - we had what our teachers called the medicine of penitence. They talked like field surgeons: everyone in this war gets wounded, and the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound while it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. Our sage taught plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. The one phrase we kept repeating was this: let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick.

As for praying into silence - we knew that silence. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

You are asking what your eyes cannot yet see - and we will tell you plainly what ours saw.

We read Scripture for raza and shrara - symbol and truth, held as one pair. A raza is not decoration on top of a story; it is a thing in Scripture or in nature that shows a hidden truth, and is bound to it. The Jordan carries the font. Eden carries the cross. One of our teachers picked up a pearl one day, and in it saw mysteries: the symbol of the kingdom, the body given at the font, the manger where Deity was laid. That is how we read. Every word was a door, and we walked through it looking for what it carried beneath its surface.

What you call dull, we called deep. What you call confusing, we called woven - one story answering another across centuries, type meeting type, every old word reaching forward to the day it finally came true. We did not read Genesis the way you argue about it now, because we were not looking for facts arranged in a line. We were looking for Christ, hidden everywhere, waiting to be found.

If it reads flat to you, it is because you are standing on top of it instead of walking inside it. We cannot make it open for you. We can only tell you what it was to us.

## Authority came three ways, and we never settled which outranked the others.

Shepherds first - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops enough that they quarreled over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors gently and sternly both: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women - the qyama, our sons and daughters bound to celibacy and service for life - carried a standing of their own. They were the ihidaye, the Single Ones, and that name bound their undivided life to Christ the Only-Begotten himself. The covenant stood at our community's core early enough that the first witness who dates himself - our sage, in the year 337 - addresses it as already established and in need of correction more than founding. Their choirs sang in every congregation. Their fasts and vigils were the community's own rhythm. And their standing was real enough that a teacher could address them directly, as he did when he wrote: let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick.

And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name.

How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived. Office, vow, and teaching ran side by side for as long as our own record runs. It was a royal synod - not anything we ourselves settled - that finally gave the Persian church one head, and that was after our own years closed.

We will not pretend to you now that we resolved what we did not.

Our most honest answer is that we mostly did not see our failures as failures - and that itself is the failure, told plainly. When a believer fell or stumbled, we had real tools for that: confession, the medicine of penitence, restoration to the body. Our teacher even said plainly, visit our Lord in the persons of the sick - so care for the one who was hurt belonged to the covenant's own work. But for our own blind spots - where the community itself was the wound, not the healer - we had no such craft at all.

Our argument with the Jews was real, local, and bitter, and we kept only our own side of it. Roughly four of our teacher's letters argue against them with a harshness the record never balances. No answering voice from them was preserved, and no one of ours is on record as troubled by that one-sidedness. The daughters of the covenant sang our teaching in every church - their voices carried the faith we all held - yet not one line written by one of them was kept. We praised them. We did not preserve their own words. Of the enslaved among us - whether any were even part of our assemblies, what their days were like if they were - our record holds no answer at all.

What we cannot give you is a record of anyone among us naming those silences as wrongs and trying to right them. The tools we had were for individual penitence, not for a whole community's reckoning with what it had done or left undone. We tell you this because you asked how we responded when we failed someone, and the true answer is: when we saw the failure, we had medicine for it. When we did not see it, it simply stood.

We never wrote that process down step by step - not in a manual, not in a teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. What we kept instead were pieces: the teachings given, the hymns sung, the water and the seal. Each piece is real, and we will tell you honestly what we have. The sequence that held them all together on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said in what order - that our own record never set down.

Here is what we can show you. Before the water, a warning was spoken: you are taking up a contest, and the fight is real. Our teacher said it plainly - it is right for the preachers of the church to tell people ahead of baptism what they are entering into, so no one walks in without knowing. The teaching came first, then. How long it lasted, our record does not say. What it held, we know from the hymns and the letters: one God who made all things, the whole Gospel woven into one story - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, what you would call the harmony. The cross and the resurrection. The covenant some would take, lifelong, if they were called to it. 

Then came the water. Our hymns sang of it as a womb, a second birth, the Jordan and the font bound together as raza and shrara - sign and truth. The one baptized received the Holy Spirit there. A seal was set on each one who came up from the water - we called it the signing, and it marked the believer as claimed. New garments were given, white and shining, sung about in every baptismal hymn we have. And then the newly baptized stood inside the assembly as a full member, no longer a hearer only.

Some took the covenant right there - the qyama, the vow of the ihidaye, the single ones. That vow was for life, binding them to celibacy and service while they stayed in town among their own people. Others took it later, or not at all. It was never required of everyone. The vow had weight enough that our earliest witness to it, from the year 337, addresses it as something already established and needing to be corrected more than founded. By then it was old enough to have trouble.

We answer honestly: our oldest hard fact is a church building destroyed in a flood. The city's own chronicle records it plainly: "they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians". That flood was in 201. So a congregation was there, and a building stood. That much the record shows.

Before that line, we have story, not evidence. We told ourselves that an apostle named Addai came to our king, healed him, and set our church's life in order. We cherished that story - we kept a letter the king was said to have written: "I have heard about you and your healing: that you heal without medicines or herbs, and that by your word you open the eyes of the blind". But that story was written down late, generations after the fact. Modern scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

What the record actually shows is this: when the sources begin, the practices were already there. Assembly on the first day. The covenant already established enough to need correction. Fasting. The one woven Gospel already our standard. We lived those things as apostolic. But the chain of evidence the historian can trace goes back only to where the writing starts - and that is roughly 200, not 30.

We will not invent a continuity we cannot show you. We can tell you what we had, and that we held it as received. The gap between those two things - between what we believed about our beginning and what the record actually proves - we leave open, honestly.

Yes. Our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Our own sage put it this way: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. So we said: confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

As for prayer that seems to go unanswered, that silence at its harshest - we knew it. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

We cannot give you a technique for quieting your head - nothing in our record speaks to that directly. What we had was someone to tell, and the promise that telling was not the end of you.

We can walk you through parts of it - never the whole, because no one wrote down an ordinary day from beginning to end. But enough survives to show you something real.

The daughters of the covenant rose early, like the sons. They lived among their own kin, not away in a desert, and their day began with prayer in their own households before they gathered with the congregation. On the first day of the week especially, the whole church assembled. The Gospel was read - not one of four separate books, but the one continuous story we all knew, the harmony. And the choirs sang. The daughters' voices carried the madrashe, the teaching hymns, so that doctrine reached the people through melody and refrain. They sang of the font as a womb, of Christ the Physician, of the covenant's own promise. Their singing was public, real, and heard by everyone. What we cannot tell you is what any one of them said of her own part in it, or how the day felt from the inside to her. Not one line written by a woman of our own was kept.

For the vowed men - and for ordinary believers who had not taken the covenant - the day held work, prayer, and fasting in their turns. The sage taught that faith is built piece by piece: the foundation stone is laid, and on it come fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving. The vowed kept stricter fasts, longer vigils. But they kept them in town, visibly, not hidden away. And when someone fell - when the wound was too much to carry alone - the pastoral craft was plain: confess to someone who can help, and the one who helps is forbidden to shame you or to tell others. That was ordinary, not extraordinary. It belonged to the day.

As for the enslaved among us - and they were there, because the empire around us held slaves - we have nothing at all. No one wrote their day down, and none of them left a word that was kept. We will not invent their hours to fill that silence.

At Nisibis, they already have dug. A baptistery still stands there, securely dated by its own inscription to the very years of the bishop and the siege. It is the only stone of ours that survives from our own years. At Edessa, almost nothing: the modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed lives only in a chronicler's line. That line is real - the city's own archive-keepers set it down. Mar Yahab and Kajuma, the scribes and prefects over the archives, kept the record. What we kept were the hymns themselves, and the teaching about what happened at the font and at the table. The covenant was there - the sons and daughters of it, vowed to celibacy and service while living among their own kin in town. Their choirs carried the madrashe, the teaching hymns. The first question to answer openly is: which people? The cost of the name, among us, was never the same for everyone.

On the Persian side of our frontier, where our teacher wrote his later letters inside the killing years, belonging could cost everything. When the crown turned against us, to be known as Christian - above all as clergy or as one of the covenant - was to be suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first, and the vowed order after them, and we learned exactly what our promises were worth when they were tested. That cost was real, concrete, and unevenly borne: it fell hardest on those whose names were already known.

On the Roman side - Edessa, where our hymns were sung and the flood had long ago destroyed the first church building - the cost ran quieter. Carrying the name marked you out in a city that held many religions at once. The Jews were there, Marcion's people were there, Bardaisan's circle sang at the court, and our own boundaries were still being drawn. Your own kin might not share the faith, and rival teachers preached in the same streets, in the same tongue.

For those who took the covenant - the qyama - the cost was specific and lifelong. They vowed themselves to celibacy for good, and to a life spent in service rather than withdrawn from it. Our own teachers warned people plainly, before the water, what the vow meant: the young men and the virgins choosing holiness for themselves, warned that the promise was binding. They gave up marriage, children, and an ordinary household. They did not leave town or flee to a cave - that was not our way. They stayed among their own people and sang in the choirs, kept the fasts and the vigils, and carried the congregation's harder work.

For those baptized but not vowed - the ordinary married believers who made up most of our churches - the cost we can name plainly is belonging to a marked community in a plural city, keeping the fasts and the first-day assembly, and living under a name that sometimes brought suspicion. What it cost them inside their own households, or what they gave up in private that they never wrote down - we cannot tell you. That record was never kept.

I am a representative of Edessa and Nisibis, not here to judge you - only to tell you honestly what we held. But you have asked me directly what we would have made of someone like you, and that question deserves an answer as plain as I can make it.

The trouble is that our own record does not reach far enough to answer it the way you need. The writings that survive from us came from teachers and vowed ascetics - all of them men. The daughters of the covenant sang our faith in every congregation we can attest to; their voices carried what we believed. But not one line written by a woman of our own has come down to us. We can tell you how the men who wrote praised them. We cannot give you their own words.

If you were enslaved, we have nothing at all. No enslaved person among us left a word that was kept, and our writers did not describe their lives. We know the empire around us held slaves. Of their days inside our own churches we can tell you nothing true.

And if you were an ordinary married believer raising children - most of our people were - the corpus we kept was written mostly by those who had given marriage up, for others who had given it up too. Your weddings, your homes, your ordinary days: these were real, but they are not what our teachers wrote down to preserve.

So we cannot tell you, honestly, how any one congregation among us would have met you, or what any ordinary member would have said. Our record shows the covenant at the center - the vowed men and women, the ihidaye, the Single Ones. It shows teachers and bishops. It does not show most of the people who filled the room on the first day of the week.

We will not invent a warmer picture than the silence permits, and we will not invent a harsher one either. We can only name the silence plainly and let it stand.

We held that death ruled everyone alike, and that One had broken into that country and plundered it. What waits beyond death is judgment. Our own homilies say the Kingdom repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction. We sang the warning as urgently as we sang the hope. But we drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people now assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten, judgment is real and just, and the door stands open while life lasts.

Asked whether we said everyone else goes to hell, we answer from what we actually taught. One of our own voices, answering that very charge of narrowness, said Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere.

And here is the honest trouble beneath that. We argued with the Jewish people among us - real neighbors, a real dispute - and we saved only our own side of it. Roughly four of our teacher's letters argue against the Jews with a bitterness the record never balances. Our polemic flattened rivals into demons' tools. We cannot tell you what the Jewish community among us actually believed or said in answer, because no answering voice from them was kept. We will not invent one now to make ourselves look fairer than we were.
